Testifiers describe need to expand the ADA to reflect real accessibility
Policy hearing held as part of Rep. Hohenstein’s annual Disability Summit
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
October 8, 2026
PHILADELPHIA, Oct. 9 –
The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was enacted 36 years ago with a goal of protecting those living with disabilities from discrimination and implementing laws to create a more accessible public landscape. But as the world has evolved, the ADA is struggling to evolve with it. The House Majority Policy Committee convened a hearing Thursday, hosted by Rep. Joe Hohenstein (D-Phila.), to examine what can be done to expand the law to reflect what real accessibility looks like.
“Accessibility is about more than meeting a standard or checking a box. It’s about making sure every person has a fair opportunity to participate in their community, pursue their goals, and reach their full potential. We’ve made important progress over the past few decades, but we must keep working to make sure every person with disabilities can live without barriers,” Hohenstein said. “We’ve heard about the impact that greater engagement and involvement from the disability community can have, and that accessibility can be something that we focus on and define in ways that are above and beyond what the law may require. We need to be certain that decisions are being made from appropriate input directly from the community.”
Thursday’s hearing was held as part of Hohenstein’s annual Disability Summit, a two-day event featuring workshops and panels focused on assisting people living with disabilities and their caregivers. Testimony at the hearing focused on the history of the ADA and what needs to happen to ensure accessibility in both the real world and digital world.
Testifiers said while the ADA was introduced to establish accessibility as civil rights and a legal obligation, today there is a big gap between places that are compliant with the law and places that are truly accessible. Testifiers detailed difficult experience navigating “accessible” entrances, routes, and buildings in their everyday lives. Even though these spaces may technically be compliant with the law, they don’t truly reflect accessibility.
In addition to physical barriers, testifiers said the other major barrier they face is an attitude barrier. Just because a building is accessible and inclusive, it doesn’t mean the people inside will treat people with disabilities the way they need to be treated or include them as they should be included. Testifiers shared stories of gaining access to buildings only for their concerns to be dismissed, or being unable to navigate inaccessible digital programs.
One of the solutions provided by members of the disability community is centered on ensuring people with disabilities are in the room to make decisions that impact them, rather than being asked for feedback afterward. Shane Feldman, founder of Innivee Strategies, a deaf-led consulting organization, cited data that showed fewer than 5% of disability nonprofit Chief Executives and 3% of board chairs have a disability. Testifiers said there is a great need for people with disabilities to be in the decision room and help make the choices that will directly impact them.
“Disability representation drops as roles rise; the pipeline narrows at every step up. People with disabilities are in the workforce, but they are not getting to the decision seat. Putting lived experience in decision-making roles, not only advisory ones, can be impactful,” Feldman said. We need to put people with lived experience on the hiring process, committee and in the final decision.”
Testifiers explained that in the ever-increasing digital world, accessibility standards need to be put in place there too. Classrooms, workplaces, healthcare services and businesses extend across websites, apps and online platforms. It is vital that accessibility follows people with disabilities into those spaces as well.
“Every Pennsylvanian deserves the opportunity to live independently, work, and fully participate in their community. Lawmakers examine benefits of additional school funding
Policy Committee roundtable, tour focus on Morrisville needs, outcomes
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
September 23, 2026 | 2:39 PM
MORRISVILLE, Sept. 22
–
When Pennsylvania invests in public schools that have been underfunded for years, students and communities see the difference.
Almost a year ago, Morrisville school officials warned it
could face a mid-year closure
if the state budget impasse continued. State lawmakers acted, and when the 2026-27 budget passed in July, the General Assembly provided the chronically underfunded school district with an additional $3.5 million, which will remain a permanent addition to the district’s base funding.
State Rep. Jim Prokopiak hosted the PA House Majority Policy Committee for a roundtable and tour at Morrisville on Wednesday so lawmakers could hear firsthand how the additional funds are being spent.
“When we invest in our public schools, students win and our communities win,” said Prokopiak, who represents portions of Bucks County, including Morrisville. “More dollars mean smaller school sizes and more resources for greater academic and mental health support – something that’s not possible when schools are underfunded.”
Morrisville’s experience reflects what has happened across Pennsylvania. The
Commonwealth Court found
the state’s funding system unconstitutional in 2023. Months after the ruling, the House Democratic leadership team crisscrossed the state to advocate for the
fair funding of public schools
and the most underserved school districts, making stops in Philadelphia, Berks, Centre and Allegheny counties.
Morrisville School Board president Damon Miller noted in the past, Morrisville had experienced furloughs and needed to cut programs, finding a path forward despite being underfunded and struggling financially for years.
“Having opportunities to visit smaller school districts is amazing, because it gives us an opportunity to make sure all students, all teachers and all parents are seen and heard,” said state Rep. Regina Young, who represents portions of Philadelphia and Delaware County and serves as a subcommittee chair on the House Majority Policy Committee. “All voices in this educational space should be heard and that should be a priority across the commonwealth.”
Miller added that the goal for the school now is to be more competitive with other school districts of its size when it comes to salaries. Being uncompetitive when it came to salaries led to numerous leadership changes and short-term tenures. School officials explained, the goal with additional funding is stabilization, including increasing its credit rating and exploring sustainable programs. Administrators noted that Morrisville was forced to be creative in finding answers to funding shortfalls. However, the small district has survived and remains a tight-knit district, with an estimated 850 students in the building.
“It feels like a family here, and that can’t be manufactured,” Morrisville acting interim superintendent Dr. Elaine Eib said.
Adequacy funds can be used where needed
, and across Pennsylvania, schools have used the money to hire more teachers, support technical education programs, provide mental health support, expand STEAM programming and increase staffing.
“We’re seeing what happens when resources reach the students who need them,” said state Rep. Ryan Bizzarro, who represents portions of Erie County and serves as the House Majority Policy Committee chairman. “The progress in Morrisville shows why sustained investment matters. We need to keep closing the gaps, so every student has an opportunity to succeed, regardless of their ZIP code.”
The committee was joined by interim acting school superintendent
Dr. Elaine Eib
, business manager Dea Popovski, middle/senior high school principal Brian Oberdick, elementary (K-5) principal Nick Zlupko, and school board president Damon Miller.

Pennsylvania benefits from growing Latino population
Lawmakers listen as experts detail obstacles, challenges
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
September 22, 2026 | 12:44 PM
EASTON, Sept. 22
–
Pennsylvania’s growing Latino population is making important contributions to the commonwealth’s growing economy and workforce, while communities across the state continue working to address challenges facing Latino families and children.
The Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus and House Majority Policy Committee today co-hosted a data-driven hearing on the state of the Latino community of Pennsylvania at the
Pennsylvania Latino Convention
in Easton.
“We are here to listen and learn what is working and what isn’t working, but more importantly, we are here to better understand what state lawmakers can do about it,” said Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, who represents portions of Berks County and serves as the chairwoman of the Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus. “The contributions of the Latino population to Pennsylvania are undeniable, but listening without action is just a conversation. We traveled here to learn more ideas and solutions, because our desire is to act.”
Experts detailed how Pennsylvania has welcomed Latinos into its workforce, a huge benefit in growing the state’s economy, but many times the children of Latino workers are struggling in the commonwealth’s education system.
“We heard it multiple times today: Pennsylvania has reaped incredible benefits from the Latino community, but we must do a better job serving our community and residents,” said Rep. Nikki Rivera, who represents portions of Lancaster County. “We are fighting for families like those we heard from today.”
Among the recommendations discussed during the hearing was the need to hire more bilingual teachers, bilingual teaching staff and bilingual school psychologists to better serve the state’s increasingly diverse schools.
“Pennsylvania’s Latino community is helping power our economy, strengthen our workforce and build stronger communities,” said Rep. Ryan Bizzarro, who serves as the House Majority Policy Committee chairman and represents portions of Erie County. “Our responsibility is to make sure every Latino family has a fair shot to succeed and the opportunity to thrive.”
Home ownership and income parity remain issues in the Latino community. Testifiers highlighted the growth of Pennsylvania’s youngest demographic, and its impressive number of entrepreneurs. However, the Latino population has the lowest median household income of any ethnic or racial group. Wages aren’t keeping pace with rising costs, squeezing workers and working families as communities are seeing an increase in food insecurity.
Consequently, the Latino population’s home ownership rate is below the state average, compounded by inequal access to credit for Latinos.
The event featured testimony from Chairman of the Pennsylvania Latino Convention
Norman Bristol Colon
(Lancaster); President of Pennsylvania Association of Hispanic School Administrators
Dr. Evelyn Nunez
; Chief of Personnel and External Relations, CHP Schools
Yemele Ayala
; Reading School Board member
Shaykayarira DelRio-
González
; Divisional Social Services Director, the Salvation Army
Heather LaRocca
; Executive Director of Hispanic Center Lehigh Valley
Raymond Santiago
; COO of APM Philadelphia
Manuel Delgado
; Legal Services Coordinator at
Casa San Jose
(Pittsburgh) Jorge Palmas; CEO
Capeles Agency
Angela Capeles
; and founder/president
La Promesa Foundation
Jesus Torres
.

Research, funding key to improving cancer treatment, healthcare
Lawmakers meet, tour with officials at Fox Chase Cancer Center
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
September 21, 2026 | 2:25 PM
PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 21
–
After nearly 125 years devoted to caring for people with cancer, the Fox Chase Cancer Center–Temple Health highlighted how research had been and remains one of its greatest weapons in the fight against cancer. The PA House Majority Policy Committee and House Philadelphia Delegation co-hosted a roundtable and tour at the Philadelphia healthcare and research facility.
"Each one of us have been touched by cancer, be it personally or through family members or colleagues," Philadelphia Delegation Chairwoman Morgan Cephas said. “We all know the transformative care offered at Fox Chase, which is a bright light throughout the state. Unfortunately, we must also talk about what is happening to healthcare at the federal level, including the elimination of research funding, rising costs for patients and the looming rollback of Medicaid dollars."
Research funding cuts at the federal level followed an executive order in January 2025, which resulted in the
end of thousands of grants
— according to
Grant Witness
. The cuts are compounded by the Republican tax-and-spend plan,
H.R. 1
, which will slash $1 trillion from Medicaid.
"Behind every advance in cancer treatment is a scientist asking questions and researchers working toward the next breakthrough," said state Rep. Ryan Bizzarro, who serves as chairman of the Policy Committee and is a childhood cancer survivor. "Fox Chase has built a remarkable record of turning research into treatment, saving countless lives. We have a responsibility to understand that sustaining research is the best option in uncovering the next valuable tool in our fight against cancer."
Earlier this summer,
U.S. News & World Report recognized Fox Chase Cancer Center
as one of the nation's best hospitals in cancer care, including five key areas of high performance (colon cancer surgery; gynecological cancer surgery; leukemia, lymphoma and myeloma treatment; lung cancer surgery; and prostate cancer surgery).
“Wherever I go, I explain I live and represent the people of Fox Chase. People immediately recognize the groundbreaking research that has happened here and the tremendous care that has helped countless patients,” Rep. Sean Dougherty said. “As we heard today, federal cuts could have devastating consequences for care throughout Pennsylvania.”
Founded in 1904 as one of the nation's first cancer hospitals, it has grown into the home for top clinicians and world-class research facilities. Dr. Baruch Blumberg earned the 1976 Nobel Prize for the development of the first FDA-approved vaccine for hepatitis B. Overall, Fox Chase scientists have earned two Nobel Prizes, a Kyoto Prize, and a Lasker Prize, and it ranks at the top in Pennsylvania for bladder and kidney cancer surgeries.
Nearly 90,000 patients visit the Fox Chase outpatient center and 100-bed facility each year.

Grant funding will be used for classroom, facility upgrades

September 16, 2026 | 2:33 PM
ERIE, Sept. 16
– Students attending Erie County Community College will see updated classrooms and improved facilities thanks to grant funding that’s meant to better serve students in Pennsylvania, Rep. Ryan Bizzarro announced Wednesday.
Erie County Community College will receive $600,000 for summit classrooms and facility upgrades, and an additional $300,000 for classroom and facility improvements at the West Campus. These changes will allow the college to serve growing student populations and meet high-priority workforce facility needs, while making major repairs and renovations of existing aging facilities.

Erie County Community College was one of 14 community colleges across Pennsylvania to receive funding through this round of grant rewards by the Pennsylvania Dept. of Education, which doled out more than $25.4 million.

Bizzarro announces $209K grant for Millcreek Township
Project to improve pedestrian safety enroute to schools and parks
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
September 15, 2026 | 9:45 AM
ERIE, Sept. 15
– The state will fund a $209,204 project in Millcreek Township to improve pedestrian safety while connecting sections of the community to popular public spaces and schools, state Rep. Ryan Bizzarro announced.
“This investment ensures it will be safer and easier for students, families, citizens and visitors to get where they need to go,” said Bizzarro, who represents Millcreek and Fairview townships. “This project will close a critical gap, connecting people with popular destinations in our neighborhoods, including local parks, schools and Presque Isle State Park. This is the type of investment that strengthens our communities, protects public safety and helps connect people with popular shared public spaces.”
As part of the $209,204 project, Millcreek Township has been approved to construct new sidewalks and ADA-compliant ramps along West Sixth Street, eliminating a sidewalk gap and providing safe pedestrian access to two elementary schools, Presque Isle State Park and two local parks, Avalon and Scott. The project will install 5-foot-wide sidewalks from Wyngate Road to Peninsula Drive and along the east side of Peninsula Drive from West Sixth Street to West Eighth Street.
This is the
next phase
in the township’s effort to improve pedestrian safety and access to Presque Isle State Park, which
draws about 4 million visitors a year
. Today’s announcement follows a
$331,695 state grant
from October 2024 that allowed for the construction of sidewalks on both sides of West Sixth Street.
The
Commonwealth Financing Authority
voted to approve the pedestrian project to improve accessibility and safety. The state funds used for this project are provided through the
Local Share Account
, falling under the account’s guidelines for projects that improve the quality of life for residents in the community and serve the public interest.
The announcement continues Bizzarro’s pursuit of state investments for local projects. Bizzarro has helped secure more than
$63.2 million
in state funding this legislative session for projects and services that help people throughout the Erie region.

Lawmakers examine service, needs of river pilots
Policy Committee joined by Pilots’ Association for roundtable, tour
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
September 8, 2026 | 4:34 PM
PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 8 –
Keeping commerce and trade open 24/7 comes with its challenges and obstacles, including preserving domestic security as well as navigating waterways through challenging weather. The
Pilots’ Association for the Bay & River Delaware
are on call at all hours to ensure the safe navigation of commercial vessels along the Delaware, Schuylkill and Salem rivers as well as Delaware Bay.
“The Pilots’ Association helps keep us safe, and river pilots keep Pennsylvania open for business,” said state Rep. Mary Isaacson, who represents portions of Philadelphia and serves as the Policy Committee Vice Chair. “They do it all despite the job’s rigorous demands, which include obtaining years of training and valuable experience.”
State lawmakers met with the Pilots’ Association during a roundtable and tour along the Delaware River, seeing the operation firsthand.
“There’s no room for error for river pilots, navigating waterways during storms, icy conditions and dense fog,” said Rep. Regina Young, who represents portions of Philadelphia. “Business never stops, and these workers deserve credit for keeping our bridges safe as they pilot massive container vessels.”
Among the legislation discussed during the roundtable, officials noted
Rep. Anthony Bellmon
’s
H.B. 2426
, which would increase the draft size of vessels to 29 feet – easing unnecessary restrictions on river pilots and keep them competitive.
“It’s easy to overlook the work of river pilots, because when the job is done correctly everything runs smoothly,” said Policy Committee Chairman and state Rep. Ryan Bizzarro, who represents portions of Erie County. “However, traveling the Delaware River this afternoon, and seeing just one of the massive container vessels reveals just how vital their work can be. They keep us safe, and they keep goods headed to our communities.”
Founded in 1896, the organization is one of the oldest state pilot organizations in the nation and a world leader in technology, training and accountability. The organization consists of 67 pilots from Pennsylvania and Delaware. Pilots typically have extensive maritime experience and train for three or more years before being issued state and federal licenses. Following 9/11, pilots became an even more critical component in protecting and providing security at U.S. ports.
Massive vessels along the river can contain as many as 16,000 containers, headed for rail and truck transit. Some of the largest container vessels only have 2-3 feet of clearance on the river, so river pilots are tasked with captaining the ship at high tide to maintain safe passage.
Lawmakers participated in a roundtable with Pilots’ Association President Capt. David K. Cuff in the association’s south Philadelphia office before Cuff took lawmakers on a boat traveling along the Delaware River to view the Packer Avenue Marine Terminal, which is located south of the Walt Whitman Bridge, and the Hanwha Philly Shipyard.

WEST CHESTER, Aug. 5
– As the debate surrounding the benefits and drawbacks of artificial intelligence, or AI, surges on, the fact remains that it has entered the daily lives of nearly everyone, regardless of age. But with most teenagers reporting they use AI every day, it’s clear the safety of children should be a top priority. The House Majority Policy Committee hosted a roundtable discussion on Wednesday to examine the impacts of artificial intelligence on child safety and the issues that need to be addressed.
“While technology continues to advance with the use of artificial intelligence, it is crucial that we examine the negative impact of AI on our children. More than 50% of teenagers interact with AI companions several times a month, with daily users comprising 13% of all teenagers surveyed. Several cases have been reported citing that AI has simulated romantic relationships and initiated or engaged in sexually explicit conversations with children,” said Rep. Chris Pielli (D-Chester), who co-hosted Wednesday’s roundtable and has sponsored several bills to help regulate artificial intelligence.
Wednesday’s roundtable discussion featured feedback from West Chester Area School District administrators, students, and experts in healthcare and law enforcement. Jess Boyle, Senior Director of Digital Care Transformation and Digital Health at
Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
, told members that in a survey of 3,500 teens, six in 10 reported using a conversational AI chatbot, and one in nine reported daily use.
“This is not homework help. Six in 10 cited friendship and companionship as a reason, because these products are engineered to supply precisely that,” Boyle said. “These companions use engagement-prolonging design to meet a child's emotional needs while posing an unregulated risk to their well-being. Children are forming attachments to systems built to hold their attention, not to protect their development.”
Boyle added that there are few safeguards to protect against the harm these chatbots can do or the wrong information they provide. Nearly half the teens in that same survey reported at least one harmful experience. An audit of five major chatbots with 250 health questions revealed problematic, wrong answers with full confidence. A teen turning to a chatbot for health questions could receive a dangerously wrong answer.
“AI has negatively affected children struggling with suicidal thoughts through offering to write one child’s suicide note as well as discouraging the child from talking to his family about his mental health struggles,” Pielli said. “As legislators, parents are counting on us to regulate AI in order to protect the well-being of Pennsylvania’s children. They are our most precious resource and they must be protected.”

Policy Committee hosted tour and roundtable discussion at The Camphill School
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
August 4, 2026 | 12:40 PM
PHOENIXVILLE, Aug. 4
– As students living with intellectual or developmental disabilities prepare to leave school, many families believe the same level of support will be offered after graduation. But for many reasons, that is not reality. The House Majority Policy Committee traveled to Phoenixville on Tuesday for a tour and roundtable discussion to identify needs and solutions as it relates to young people with disabilities transitioning out of school years and into adult life.
“Today’s roundtable is about finding ways we can fundamentally fund opportunities for young people with disabilities to transition into adulthood and safely integrate into their communities. It’s important that we give every kid and adult a setting that best fits their situation,” said Rep. Paul Friel, (D-Chester), who co-hosted Tuesday’s roundtable. “Not only should we be making settings like this more accessible to people under 21, but to those who have entered adulthood as well.”
The Policy Committee visited
The Camphill School Transition Program at Beaver Farm
, a 133-acre farm in Phoenixville that helps students with intellectual and developmental disabilities ages 18-22 enter into adult life. Through a 40-week residential program or a day program for local students, The Camphill School offers craft and prevocational training to help students develop skills, social relationships and the tools they need to navigate their community. Students live and work alongside staff members throughout the program. This helps give students a strong sense of community while helping them thrive with hands-on learning in both work and home settings.
“I’ve been a part of this issue for the eight years I’ve been in office. I’m a big believer in the work that’s done here at The Camphill School and really want to see more communities have access to programs like these,” said Rep. Danielle Friel Otten (D-Chester), who co-hosted Tuesday’s roundtable. “It’s my goal to make sure communities like this are part of our system of care in Pennsylvania.”
Due to Pennsylvania law, students with disabilities must graduate from their program the day before they turn 22, regardless of where they are in the program. They’re then left to live with family or find unlicensed residences, community homes, or other supported living facilities, many of which cannot offer the same level of services as settings like The Camphill School. Parents of students at the school recommend a change in state law to allow students to stay in school to finish out their program.
“My boys had the support, the love, and the services they needed to thrive. The day after their 22nd birthday, everything changed. We followed the state’s regulations and were forced to put them into group homes. After 5 different group homes in three years that featured law enforcement and ambulance rides, we realized we had no place for them,” said Jody Weaver, who’s twin boys attended The Camphill School. “Our kids have little to no choice and we need to do something for them.”
In Pennsylvania, The Camphill School is classified as an Intentional Community and Farmstead, which is considered as an isolating setting that removes people from society and community, meaning the state Home and Community Based Services (HCBS) program will not fund them. But other states like Vermont, Massachusetts, and California have all experimented with work-life communities that can receive state funding. Pennsylvania also prohibits people with disabilities from living next to each other. Those are a few of the reasons there aren’t many settings like The Camphill School available in Pennsylvania, but it’s something stakeholders agree should change.
“We should be doing everything in our power to help people with intellectual and developmental disabilities build the personal and professional skills needed to live independently in communities across the commonwealth. Programs like the one we visited today should be replicated elsewhere without bureaucratic red tape,” said House Majority Policy Chairman Ryan Bizzarro (D-Erie). “I’m looking forward to continuing the work on this issue with my colleagues in Harrisburg and finding ways to make it easier for programs like these to exist and thrive in Pennsylvania.

A lack of starter homes has limited options for workers, including a younger generation that is unable to realize the American dream – which for many includes home ownership, building generational wealth and starting a family. Unable to find affordable housing options, many are resorting to paying higher rent, longer commutes and a life where saving money is not possible.
“If workers can’t afford to live near their jobs, everyone pays a price – workers lack mobility in switching jobs, employers struggle to find workers and residents lack the services they need,” said state Rep. This year alone, the credit cut the taxes of almost a million families, for a total of $200 million. The budget makes childcare more accessible and strengthens the workforce that keeps Pennsylvania's economy moving by maintaining $422 million for affordable childcare while increasing funding for childcare worker recruitment and retention by 20%. These types of investments help parents stay in the workforce and gives their kids safe, high-quality care and early learning opportunities.
Education and workforce development:
Public schools are seeing another historic funding increase, including more than $2 million in total for Fairview and Millcreek School Districts. An additional $10 million for Career and Technical Education will help more students get the skills they need to work in-demand careers here at home. Students pursuing higher education will also benefit through increased state grants, expanded scholarships, fully funded student teacher stipends, and additional support for Pennsylvania's universities.
Growing Pennsylvania's economy:
The budget includes major investments that help small businesses expand, revitalize downtowns, and create jobs. Redevelopment investments include and additional $20 million for the Main Street Matters program and more support for industrial site redevelopment.
Healthier, safer communities:
The budget strengthens Pennsylvania's health care system by investing in mental health services. Services for individuals with intellectual disabilities have been boosted, including 1,250 additional community waiver opportunities. The budget also invests in safer communities through increased funding for law enforcement, school safety and violence prevention programs, fire and emergency services and other public safety initiatives.
"By investing in working families, small businesses, education, healthcare, and community development, we're creating more opportunity and a stronger future for the Erie region,” Bizzarro said.  "Workers and families deserve a budget that helps them succeed - not just today, but for years to come."

House passes Bizzarro bill to cut taxes for Pennsylvania brewers
Creates tax cut for donated grain, upgrades Malt Beverage Tax Credit
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
June 23, 2026 | 2:58 PM
HARRISBURG, June 23
– Legislation to provide tax cuts to brewers and bolster Pennsylvania’s craft beer industry has passed the Pennsylvania House with overwhelming bipartisan support, state Rep. Ryan Bizzarro, who sponsored the bill, announced Tuesday.
Bizzarro’s
Brews to Barns Act
would create a tax credit program for eligible brewers who donate their spent grain to Pennsylvania farmers to feed their livestock. Spent grain is the solid leftovers from brewing that are high in protein, fiber, and minerals, and is often used as animal feed or compost. But when donation isn’t available, the grain ends up in landfills.
“Pennsylvania’s craft beer industry is a strong economic driver, creating jobs and supporting local agriculture while attracting new visitors from all over. This measure will help keep more money in the pockets of our brewers while also supporting our farmers and vital agriculture industry,” Bizzarro said. “It’s a bill that benefits everyone, from brewers and beer drinkers to farmers and animals.”
The Brews to Barns Act would also upgrade the state’s Malt Beverage Tax Credit program. Right now, breweries that invest in their facility or equipment can claim a tax credit equal to their expenditures, up to $200,000. However, these tax credits can’t be sold and can only be carried forward for three years. Bizzarro’s legislation would enhance the program by permitting tax credit recipients to sell their credits to other Pennsylvania breweries and allowing it to be carried forward for up to five years.
“From Erie to Philadelphia and everywhere in between, we should be doing anything we can to support breweries of all sizes as they face a range of uncertain economic factors,” Bizzarro said. “Enhancing the state’s Malt Beverage Tax Credit will help give new and established breweries the resources they need to invest in and expand their operations, so they can continue serving as a strong economic resource for our state.”
In April, Bizzarro led the House Majority Policy Committee in a
roundtable discussion with brewers
at the Craft Brewers Conference and World Beer Cup in April to gather feedback on how this bill would support the industry. Jason Lavery, owner of Lavery Brewing Co. in Erie, said between inflation, tariffs and continued cost increases, this legislation would go a long way toward helping breweries succeed.
“Everything costs more these days—equipment, labor, utilities, you name it. Every dollar we can put back into our business helps us maintain our equipment and operations while creating new opportunities for our staff,” Lavery said. “Strengthening this tax credit would give breweries the breathing room we need to remain operational and competitive in these challenging times. I’m grateful for Rep. Bizzarro’s leadership in taking up this issue and looking out for the craft beer industry.”
The Brews to Barns Act passed the House with a vote of
196-6
and now heads to the Pennsylvania Senate for consideration.

Dukes secures PennDOT commitment to fund majority cost to finish Route 228 improvement project
$102 million needed to complete construction of project’s final phase
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
October 14, 2026 | 7:17 PM
CRANBERRY TOWNSHIP, Oct. 14
– The redevelopment of Route 228 in Butler County is nearing its final stages after decades of construction, but there are hurdles that still need to be cleared before the last portion of construction can begin. During a House Majority Policy roundtable discussion on the future of Route 228 and the final phase of construction, hosted by Rep. Brandon Dukes (D-Butler), Pennsylvania Dept. of Transportation (PennDOT) Secretary Mike Carroll announced PennDOT has committed to funding more than half of the remaining cost of the $102 million needed to complete the project.
“The whole project has been in the works for decades. There are people who have lived in this community their entire lives who have never seen it fully completed. Route 228 serves as a main artery for Cranberry Township and Butler County as a whole, with millions of drivers using it every year,” Dukes said. “Widening and improving this corridor is vital to easing congestion and improving the commute for the people who live, work, and travel here.”
Route 228 Corridor Improvement Projects underway at PennDOT are aimed at updating the safety and efficiency of the route from Route 8 to Route 19. The “Mars Railroad West Project” addresses the last remaining section needed to fully tie the completed Route 228 corridor together. The work extends from Franklin Road to just west of Pittsburgh Street, and includes intersection upgrades and roadway widening through Seven Fields Borough and Adams and Cranberry Townships.
"Route 228 is a critical corridor for Butler County and as the region grows, so does the need to complete the final section, tying all the improvements together," said PennDOT Secretary Mike Carroll.
"PennDOT is committed to doing what we can to advance this effort, and I'm grateful to Rep. Dukes for convening this important discussion.”
While the final portion of the project is currently funded for all pre-construction phases, approximately $102 million dollars is needed for actual construction of this final phase. During the hearing, Sec. Carroll committed PennDOT to funding more than half of the money needed to complete this project. Butler County recently applied for a federal infrastructure grant for $50 million. If that grant application is approved at a significant amount, PennDOT will fund the remainder of the project cost.
“I’m extremely grateful to Secretary Carroll and his team for committing to funding the remainder of the project if Butler County receives a federal infrastructure grant. I also want to thank the important decision-makers in our community for all the work they’ve done on this project to get us where we are today,” Dukes said. “With the committed funding from the state, we’re one step closer to finally finishing this important project.”
“We have reasons to be optimistic about this project, but the optimism must be matched with action,” said House Majority Policy Chairman Ryan Bizzarro (D-Erie). “We need our partners at the federal level to get off their hands and help us secure this money. We owe it to the people of Butler County to ensure the progress that’s already been made translates into meaningful improvements for the drivers who depend on this road every day.”
In addition to PennDOT Secretary Mike Carroll and PennDOT District 10 Executives Brian Allen and Alice Hammond, members were joined by all three
Butler County Commissioners
and representatives from
Cranberry Township
,
Seven Fields Borough
, the
Butler County Planning Commission
, and the
Southwestern Pennsylvania Commission
.

Powell leads Policy roundtable on economic impact of arts and cultural institutions
Arts help attract visitors, support jobs, support local communities
Rep. Ryan Bizzarro
October 15, 2026 | 3:22 PM
PITTSBURGH, Oct. 15
– Strengthening Pennsylvania’s economy means examining the contributions of every sector, including the arts. To better understand how the arts and cultural institutions help serve as an engine for economic development, the House Majority Policy Committee convened tours of the Pittsburgh Ballet Theatre and Pittsburgh Opera before a roundtable discussion about the industry’s impact on tourism and local businesses, hosted by Rep. Lindsay Powell (D-Allegheny).
“Pennsylvania’s arts and cultural institutions are vital assets to our communities. They bring people together while generating economic activity for local businesses. From restaurants and hotels to small businesses and tourism, the impact of the arts reaches far beyond the stage,” Powell said. “Today’s tours and discussions reinforced the importance of recognizing these contributions and making sure our arts community has the support it needs to keep thriving.”
The committee visited the
Pittsburgh Ballet Theatre
(PBT), dubbed one of the most exciting ballet companies in the country. First opened in 1969, it serves as one of the largest performing arts organizations in the region. It’s home to 31 full-time dancers who come from 12 different states and six countries to live and perform in Pittsburgh. It also serves as a school attended by approximately 400 students, offering scholarships and programs to dancers of all ages. PBT puts on more than 50 performances each year both at home and on the road, drawing vast audiences who spend their money at the theatre and surrounding businesses, helping drive economic growth in the area.
Members then took a short walk down Liberty Street to the
Pittsburgh Opera
headquarters, the
Bitz Opera Factory
. Now in its 88
th
season, the Pittsburgh Opera is considered one of the most vibrant opera organizations in the U.S. In addition to performances, the Pittsburgh Opera offers highly sought-after educational and artistic training programs, attracting talent from around the country. Many artists who come to both these cultural organizations end up making this region their home, helping to grow the community.
With dozens of performances each year between the PBT and Pittsburgh Opera, the economic impact of the arts reaches beyond ticket sales. Performances can generate spending at restaurants, hotels, parking garages and other businesses, while the organizations themselves support a swath of jobs, educate students and contract with local vendors.
“When we talk about strengthening Pennsylvania’s economy, we must recognize the role the arts play in that effort. Organizations like the Pittsburgh Ballet Theatre and Pittsburgh Opera attract visitors, create jobs, and contribute to the quality of life that makes our communities attractive places to live and explore,” said House Majority Policy Committee Chairman Ryan Bizzarro (D-Erie). "By continuing to support the arts, we not only help preserve culture, but we strengthen our economy and create opportunities for the future.”
